title: System Architecture & Deployment Quiz
description: Test your system design knowledge: microservices, CI/CD, Kubernetes, circuit breakers, Saga pattern, and GitOps.

questions.text: What is the primary difference between a monolithic and a microservices architecture?

options.text: A monolith uses containers; microservices do not
A monolith is deployed as a single unit; microservices are deployed as independent services
Microservices must share a single database; a monolith cannot
A monolith can only run on one server; microservices run on many

questions.explanation: In a monolithic architecture all functionality is bundled and deployed together, while microservices decompose the application into independently deployable services.

questions.text: Which HTTP method is conventionally used to UPDATE an existing resource in a REST API?

options.text: POST
GET
PUT
DELETE

questions.explanation: PUT (or PATCH for partial updates) is the RESTful convention for updating an existing resource identified by its URI.

questions.text: In one sentence, what does Docker do?

options.text: It provisions virtual machines on cloud providers
It packages an application and its dependencies into a portable container that runs consistently anywhere
It replaces the operating system kernel for better performance
It orchestrates clusters of servers across data centers

questions.explanation: Docker uses OS-level virtualisation to package code and its runtime into lightweight, reproducible containers.

questions.text: What does CI/CD stand for?

options.text: Container Integration / Container Delivery
Continuous Inspection / Continuous Deployment
Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery (or Deployment)
Code Integration / Code Distribution

questions.explanation: CI/CD stands for Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery (or Deployment), automating build, test, and release pipelines.

questions.text: Why are environment variables preferred over hard-coded values for secrets in an application?

options.text: They make the application run faster
They keep sensitive values out of source code and allow configuration per environment
They are automatically encrypted at the OS level
They are required by the Docker runtime

questions.explanation: Externalising secrets as environment variables prevents them being committed to version control and allows the same image to run in dev, staging, and production.

questions.text: What is the main job of a load balancer?

options.text: Compressing HTTP responses before they reach the client
Distributing incoming network traffic across multiple servers
Caching database query results
Monitoring application logs in real time

questions.explanation: A load balancer routes incoming requests across a pool of servers to maximise throughput, minimise latency, and avoid overloading any single node.

questions.text: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?

options.text: Horizontal scaling adds more CPU/RAM to a single server; vertical scaling adds more servers
Horizontal scaling adds more servers; vertical scaling adds more CPU/RAM to an existing server
They are the same concept but used in different cloud providers
Horizontal scaling only applies to databases; vertical scaling only applies to web servers

questions.explanation: Scaling out (horizontal) means adding more instances, while scaling up (vertical) means increasing the resources of an existing instance.

questions.text: When Nginx is used as a reverse proxy, which traffic direction does it primarily handle?

options.text: Requests from internal services to the database
Outbound requests from the server to external APIs
Inbound client requests forwarded to backend application servers
Traffic between microservices inside a Kubernetes cluster

questions.explanation: A reverse proxy like Nginx sits in front of backend servers, receiving client requests and forwarding them to the appropriate upstream service.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a health check endpoint (e.g., GET /health) in a web service?

options.text: To return the current CPU and memory usage to the end user
To allow load balancers and orchestrators to verify that the service is running correctly
To trigger a manual restart of the service
To expose internal API documentation

questions.explanation: Health check endpoints give orchestration tools like Kubernetes and load balancers a reliable signal to decide whether traffic should be sent to a given instance.

questions.text: In a deployment pipeline, what does a rollback accomplish?

options.text: It deletes all data written since the last release
It reverts the running application to a previously known-good version
It scales the number of instances back to zero
It resets environment variables to their default values

questions.explanation: A rollback redeploys a previous stable artifact or image when the current release is found to be defective.

questions.text: The 12-Factor App methodology's 'Config' factor states that configuration should be stored in:

options.text: A config file committed alongside the source code
The environment
A dedicated configuration microservice
A relational database table

questions.explanation: Factor III of the 12-Factor App says anything that varies between deploys (credentials, resource handles) must be stored in environment variables, not in code.

questions.text: In a blue/green deployment, what happens to the 'blue' environment after a successful switch to 'green'?

options.text: It is permanently deleted to save cost
It continues to receive 50 % of production traffic
It is kept idle and can serve as a rollback target
It is automatically upgraded to match the green environment

questions.explanation: The old blue environment remains on standby so that traffic can be instantly switched back if a critical defect is discovered in green.

questions.text: What differentiates a canary deployment from a blue/green deployment?

options.text: Canary deployments require two identical environments; blue/green requires only one
Canary deployments gradually shift a small percentage of traffic to the new version before a full rollout
Canary deployments are only used for database migrations
Blue/green deployments are always faster than canary deployments

questions.explanation: A canary release exposes the new version to a small slice of users first, allowing teams to catch problems with limited blast radius before rolling out fully.

questions.text: In Kubernetes, what is the role of a Pod?

options.text: It is the control plane component that schedules containers onto nodes
It is the smallest deployable unit, wrapping one or more co-located containers that share network and storage
It is the Kubernetes equivalent of a virtual machine
It is the configuration manifest for a Kubernetes cluster

questions.explanation: A Pod is Kubernetes's atomic unit of deployment — containers within the same Pod share an IP address, localhost network, and mounted volumes.

questions.text: What is the key difference between DNS-based and registry-based service discovery?

options.text: DNS-based discovery works only inside a single host; registry-based works across hosts
DNS-based discovery resolves service names to IPs via standard DNS; registry-based services query a dedicated registry (e.g., Consul) for live instance lists
Registry-based discovery is slower because it requires a round trip to the registry on every request
There is no practical difference — both achieve exactly the same result

questions.explanation: DNS-based discovery leverages standard DNS records for routing, while client-side registry discovery queries a service like Consul or Eureka to get a fresh list of healthy instances.

questions.text: What problem does an API gateway pattern solve in a microservices architecture?

options.text: It replaces the need for a message broker between services
It provides a single entry point for clients, handling cross-cutting concerns like auth, rate limiting, and routing
It synchronises databases across services automatically
It eliminates the need for service health checks

questions.explanation: An API gateway acts as the front door for all client requests, centralising concerns such as authentication, SSL termination, and request routing away from individual services.

questions.text: Why should microservices be designed to be stateless?

options.text: Stateless services run faster because they never write to disk
Stateless services can be freely scaled out and replaced without migrating session data
Stateless services do not need a load balancer
Kubernetes only supports stateless workloads

questions.explanation: When a service holds no local state, any instance can handle any request, making horizontal scaling and fault recovery straightforward.

questions.text: In the circuit breaker pattern, what does the 'Half-Open' state represent?

options.text: The circuit is permanently disabled and traffic is rejected
The circuit allows a limited number of test requests through to see whether the downstream service has recovered
The circuit is passing all traffic normally after a successful recovery
The circuit is blocked but still logging requests for audit purposes

questions.explanation: The Half-Open state is a probe phase: a small number of requests are forwarded; if they succeed the circuit closes again, otherwise it re-opens.

questions.text: How does the token bucket algorithm differ from the leaky bucket algorithm for rate limiting?

options.text: Token bucket enforces a strict constant output rate; leaky bucket allows bursts up to the bucket capacity
Token bucket allows bursts up to the bucket capacity; leaky bucket enforces a strict constant output rate
They are identical — just different names used by different vendors
Leaky bucket is only used for UDP traffic; token bucket is for HTTP

questions.explanation: Token bucket accumulates tokens over time and permits bursts by spending multiple tokens at once, whereas leaky bucket drains at a fixed rate regardless of input speed.

questions.text: What does 'immutable infrastructure' mean?

options.text: Servers are patched in place and never restarted
Servers are never modified after deployment; changes are applied by replacing instances with new ones built from updated images
Infrastructure configuration files are stored in a read-only S3 bucket
All servers in a cluster must have identical hardware specifications

questions.explanation: Immutable infrastructure treats servers like disposable artefacts: instead of patching live hosts, you build a new image and roll out fresh instances, eliminating configuration drift.

questions.text: Why does a rolling update in Kubernetes use readiness probes before routing traffic to new pods?

options.text: To check that the container image was signed by a trusted registry
To ensure the new pod is fully initialised and ready to serve requests before old pods are removed
To throttle the deployment speed to avoid overwhelming the scheduler
To run database migrations inside the new pod before traffic is sent

questions.explanation: Kubernetes gates traffic on readiness probes to guarantee zero-downtime rolling updates — a pod only joins the load balancer rotation once it passes the probe.

questions.text: What is the expand-contract (parallel change) pattern for database migrations?

options.text: Run a full database backup before and after every schema change
First expand the schema to support both old and new shapes, deploy code that works with both, then contract the schema by removing the old shape
Scale the database cluster horizontally before applying a migration, then scale it back down afterwards
Use feature flags to hide new columns from users until the migration is complete

questions.explanation: Expand-contract decouples schema changes from code deployments so both old and new application versions can run simultaneously, enabling zero-downtime migrations.

questions.text: In the context of distributed systems, what does API idempotency guarantee?

options.text: A request will always be processed in under 100 ms
Making the same request multiple times produces the same result as making it once
The API will automatically retry failed requests on behalf of the client
Each request is processed by exactly one server instance

questions.explanation: Idempotency is essential for safe retries in unreliable networks — if the client cannot tell whether a request succeeded, re-sending it must not cause duplicate side effects.

questions.text: In the Saga pattern, what is the key difference between choreography and orchestration?

options.text: Choreography uses a central coordinator to call each service in order; orchestration uses events emitted by each service
Choreography has each service react to domain events and publish new ones; orchestration uses a central saga orchestrator to command each step
Choreography is only used for read operations; orchestration is only for write operations
They are equivalent implementations with different naming conventions

questions.explanation: In choreography services communicate through events with no central brain, while in orchestration a dedicated process explicitly drives each step and handles compensating transactions.

questions.text: The Strangler Fig pattern is used to:

options.text: Gradually replace a legacy monolith by routing specific features to new microservices until the monolith can be retired
Throttle traffic to a legacy system to force users onto a new platform faster
Inject faults into a legacy system to find hidden dependencies before migration
Wrap a legacy database with an ORM to decouple it from the application layer

questions.explanation: Inspired by the strangler fig tree, the pattern intercepts calls to the old system and redirects them incrementally to new services until the legacy system can be decommissioned.

questions.text: What is the primary goal of chaos engineering tools like Chaos Monkey and Gremlin?

options.text: To stress-test databases by generating millions of random write operations
To proactively inject failures into production systems to expose weaknesses before they cause unplanned outages
To simulate high network latency during load testing in staging environments only
To fuzz API inputs and detect security vulnerabilities in microservices

questions.explanation: Chaos engineering deliberately introduces turbulence — killing instances, dropping network packets, exhausting CPU — to verify that a system's resilience mechanisms work before a real incident occurs.

questions.text: What does a service mesh like Istio or Linkerd provide that a traditional API gateway does not?

options.text: A single external entry point for all client-facing HTTP traffic
Mutual TLS, traffic observability, and fine-grained routing between every service-to-service call inside the cluster
Automatic horizontal pod autoscaling based on network throughput
DNS resolution for services that span multiple Kubernetes namespaces

questions.explanation: A service mesh operates at the east-west (service-to-service) layer via sidecar proxies, providing mTLS encryption, circuit breaking, and telemetry for all internal communication — beyond what a north-south API gateway handles.

questions.text: In GitOps (using ArgoCD or Flux), what is the single source of truth for the desired cluster state?

options.text: The running containers in the Kubernetes cluster
A Git repository containing declarative infrastructure and application manifests
The CI pipeline's most recently published artifact
An operations runbook stored in a wiki

questions.explanation: GitOps mandates that a Git repository is the authoritative record of desired state; the GitOps controller continuously reconciles the live cluster to match what is declared in that repo.

questions.text: In a multi-region active-active architecture, which consistency challenge must be explicitly addressed?

options.text: Ensuring all regions use the same container image digest
Handling write conflicts and replication lag when the same data can be modified concurrently in different regions
Routing all writes through a single primary region to avoid latency
Synchronising Kubernetes node clocks across regions via NTP

questions.explanation: Active-active setups allow writes in every region, so the system must implement a conflict-resolution strategy (e.g., last-write-wins, CRDTs, or vector clocks) and tolerate transient replication lag.

questions.text: Which three pillars make up full observability in a distributed system, and why are correlation IDs important?

options.text: Uptime, latency, and error rate; correlation IDs link SLO alerts to on-call schedules
Logs, metrics, and traces; correlation IDs allow a single request to be tracked end-to-end across all services and their telemetry
Dashboards, alerts, and runbooks; correlation IDs replace the need for distributed tracing
CPU, memory, and disk; correlation IDs map infrastructure metrics to application deployments

questions.explanation: Logs, metrics, and distributed traces are the three observability pillars; a correlation ID propagated through every service call ties all three signals together, making it possible to reconstruct the full journey of a request across a microservices system.

You understand not just what these patterns are but why they exist and what trade-offs they carry. You are the person teams turn to when designing for reliability, scalability, and observability. Whether you are architecting a greenfield platform or safely decomposing a legacy monolith, your decisions are grounded in deep, practical knowledge. The industry needs architects like you.
